newsitem.title: UK: ICCO to meet, hopes to agree on reserve fund money.
newsitem.headline: ICCO to meet, hopes to agree on reserve fund money.

text.p: International Cocoa Organization (ICCO) members hope to hammer out details of a special reserve fund at a three-day meeting in London from Wednesday after funding for it ended in deadlock at the group's last meeting in March.

The three-million-stg special reserve fund, used to pay ICCO expenses, has been about evenly split between member contributions and buffer stock sales. But buffer stocks are expected to be liquidated by April 1998, which means the ICCO will have to find another way to meet the shortfall.

"That gap can be plugged by cutting back the activities and the size of the organization," said a consumer spokesman. "It can also be plugged by increasing members' contributions to fill the gap. But to help ease the pain a bit, it was decided to set up some kind of reserve fund, which would generate some interest which can be put into the budget and thereby, help matters."
He said "in March, we agreed to set up a reserve of three million pounds. And the first 1.5 million has been sorted out. That was just made up of money coming straight from buffer stock funds."
"The second 1.5 million has got to be sorted out. Ideally, this week but certainly by September at the latest," he said.

If the matter is resolved by September, the fund can be established before talks start on future ICCO budgets and the amount of money and interest earned can be worked out when figuring future members' contributions. The current agreement does not expire until September 1999.

Producers hope to split the remaining 1.5 million pounds equally with consumers, "but there is a sticking point, which is the method of calculating individual countries' contributions," the spokesman said, adding "I think the principle will be agreed, but the details still require some thinking about."
In March, Brazil blocked a decision because it wanted the fund decoupled from buffer stock revenues estimated at a total $300 million, of which Brazil has the largest entitlement.
Producers contributed 80 percent of the money gathered for buffer stocks in the 1970s, and Brazil was reluctant to forgo any of its share.
Hagen Streichert, German delegate and consumer spokesman, said he hoped Brazil would step down from its position.

Other discussions include a review of Common Fund project proposals, including improving cocoa marketing in Africa. The Common Fund said the project is worth pursuing but is expensive at a preliminary estimated cost of $17 million.
"I'm sceptical that we will be able to finalise these project proposals," Streichert said. "I feel this fish is a little too big for our mouth."

A cocoa tree stocks project to find out how much cocoa is being grown and can be grown in the future will also be discussed. But the spokesman said the Common Fund is not really in favour of supporting it so producing countries are looking to see if they can get financing from elsewhere. --Medora Lee, London newsroom +44 171 542 8072
